utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we please have the appearances for today starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, with my colleagues Carolyn Edgerton, Carmela Javier, and Mr. Salvatore Cannata.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Novak Lukic and Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I guess you're calling a new witness, Mr. -- is it Madam Edgerton? Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One more appearance this week in front of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, this witness, my next witness who I met for the first time this morning raised a matter relating to protective measures, which she hadn't previously raised in contacts with officials of the OTP or the Victim/Witness Unit, and I've just a further conversation with her, and she's asked me to address the measures in front of Your Honours. So I wonder if we might move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thought Madam Usher was bringing the witness. Now, that's a very interesting witness who is walking in. Can somebody help?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On behalf of the witness and myself, I do appreciate Your Honours' and my friends' patience and understanding in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. May I raise an issue while we're waiting for the witness? Given the fact that we started after 3.00 today, may I suggest that we sit for one and a half hour sessions and have one break. Then we'll finish exactly at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, ma'am. You may be seated. Before your attorney starts talking to you, let me just say to you that your attorney told us that you were asking for protective measures of face distortion. Such measures have been granted. You can feel free to testify. Your face will not be shown to the public, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your name for the Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Slavica Livnjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Livnjak, this morning preparing for your testimony here today, do you remember that my colleagues read back to you the contents of statements you gave to police from your own country?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you understand everything that they read to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was in your own language?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you remember them reading back to you the contents of statements you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, as well, one in 1995 and one in 2005?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you understood everything in those statements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was in your own language?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I understand that you wish to make two clarifications with respect to the information in those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can we just say, was it -- the second statement, was it 2005 or 2006?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 2005, Your Honour. That's the information I have here before me. If you'll indulge me for a second. The information I have is not correct, and it was in fact 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Livnjak, as I understand it you wish to clarify two things with respect to the information contained in those statements. One was that in your statement to police from your country in 1995 when you talked about the people who were wounded in the sniping incident, that description wasn't correct; and the description of the people wounded and injured that appeared in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006 was. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was in paragraph 9 of your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006 where the correct information was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also wanted to clarify that at the intersection where the tram you were driving was shot, there were two UNPROFOR vehicles positioned, and they were there every day, and that if they weren't there the trams wouldn't have driven; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honours, if I could have the witness's statements at 65 ter number 9264 and 9265 admitted as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter number numbers 9264 and 9265 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 9264 will become Exhibit P31; and 65 ter 09265 will become Exhibit P32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, a further question. This morning in preparing for your testimony today, did my colleagues read back to you in your own language the questions my former colleague Mr. John Docherty asked of you in the Dragomir Milosevic trial and the answers you gave him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did they also read back to you the questions asked by my friend Mrs. Isailovic and the answers you gave her?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I was to ask you all those same questions today as Mr. Docherty and Mrs. Isailovic, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you also have a chance to look at copies of photographs of the location at which your tram was at when it was shot that you marked when you last appeared in front of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you have any corrections or changes to the markings you made on those photographs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, if I may, the Prosecution would like to move 65 ter numbers 9268 - being the transcript of testimony of the witness - and the associated exhibits referred to in her testimony in chief and cross-examination - those are ter numbers 9266, 9267, and 4380 - into evidence as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Those 65 ter documents are admitted into evidence. May they please be given exhibit numbers starting with 9268.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 9268 will become Exhibit P33, Your Honours; 9266 will become Exhibit P34; 9267 will become Exhibit P35; and 04380 will become Exhibit P36, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That evidence having been admitted, Your Honours, if I may, I'd like to read a brief summary of what that comprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, this witness is going to and has given evidence in respect of scheduled incident B11 of this indictment. Mrs. Livnjak has been a tram driver in Sarajevo since 1977. Around midday on 3 March 1995, she was driving a crowded tram filled with civilians on the tram route along Zmaja od Bosne from the depot towards the old town of Sarajevo. This was a time of cease-fire. The witness stated that the most dangerous place on the tram line which came under constant sniper fire was the area close to the Holiday Inn where the tram makes two turns on a very short distance. She described this as an S curve. Tram drivers have to reduce speed to be able to navigate the S curve safely. On the day in question, as she neared this area the witness saw the pentograph on another tram a few metres ahead of her hit by gunfire as it was taking the bend. As her tram hit the curve, it was also hit by gunfire coming from the right-hand side. Passengers shouted that people had been injured, and Mrs. Livnjak drove to cover behind the Executive Council building where people got out. She saw some of the wounded passengers. She stated there were no military targets in the area of the tram at the time of the incident. The witness believes the gunshots came from the Metalka building, which she described as a well-known sniper position in an area held by forces of the army of Republika Srpska. The Metalka building was the only place the shots could have come from. She marked aerial photographs illustrating the location at which her tram was at the time it was shot and the building she identified as the source of fire. She gave evidence that she saw no military combat going on near the tram at the time it was shot, nor were there any Bosnian army troops or military facilities in the area. And that's the summary of her evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I have no further questions for this witness than what you've heard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just before I turn you over to the counsel for the Defence, let me just clear one little point with you, Witness. From 1977 to 1993 where were you driving trams? I know it's a small issue. Just ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sarajevo. Ilidza, Bascarsija; Bascarsija, Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought in your statement of April 2006, you said trams started operating in Sarajevo for the first time during the war in March 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the war zones, yes. While the war was going on, the trams started running in March 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh. This was not the first time they were operating in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand your question. How do you mean the first time? There's been a tram in Sarajevo for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just reading what was written in your statement. The trams started operating in Sarajevo for the first time during the war in March 1994. Paragraph 6, the very last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Lukic one of the Defence counsels for Mr. Perisic. I'm going to ask you a few questions now. Now to be precise with respect to the question Judge Moloto just asked you: Before the war in Bosnia, that is to say before 1992, the trams ran normally, and that was the line from Ilidza towards the centre of town and towards the Miljacka River. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the conflict began, the trams stopped working until March 1994 as you said in your statement, and then it started operating again on that particular line, the line that had existed previously. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but not the whole line. It wasn't operational along the whole route, the whole line. It just worked for a brief distance, and then as the network was set up again it would go further on to Skenderija and then from Skenderija to Carsija, the centre of the town. Then we went Bascarsija and the depot, and that was the circle line that was operational during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember how many trams were working? We're talking about the period from March 1994 and then during the conflict. So the time when the trams were running, how many trams were running?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: There were six trams at the beginning when we had this reduced schedule. One tram went from Cengic Vila and the depot, and the other went from Alipasin bridge, Alipasino, and then forwards and backwards. They reversed. Now, as the network expanded, the trams were renewed and the number of trams increased until we had the whole depot Bascarsija line, the circle line, and then there were about 20 trams running. I'm not quite sure of the exact number but either 18 or 20, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's simplify this. In the period of March 1995 - let's take that for example - at how many minutes would the tram pass by towards the Holiday Inn, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Let me tell you this way: It depended on the driver driving that particular tram. If the driver drove the tram slowly, then there would be a longer time between the two trams. If the drivers were quicker, then that interval would be reduced; but otherwise, normally it would be every four minutes. There would be a tram every four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 2006, you said that after the incident of the 3rd of March the trams were not operational for three days and then they started working again. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, it seems to me, or perhaps I didn't understand the translation we received when the Prosecutor read out the summary of your statement, but I understood it this way: On the day that the incident broke out, you were driving from the depot towards Bascarsija and the centre of town. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it, too, when the statement was read out, but I think that perhaps on page 11 of the transcript that wasn't stated in precise terms. Anyway, the Miljacka River, if you were moving in your direction, the river was to your right; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, to make things clear to everyone in the courtroom, I'd like to ask the usher to have put up on e-court 65 ter, the map, 4448, map number 4448. But we're going to zoom in onto the right-hand side in relation to the areas we were looking at with yesterday's witnesses. So I'm going to ask you whether you can find your way around the map; and if you can find your way, I'll ask you some questions. If you can't find your way and get your bearings, please tell me. While we're waiting for the map to come up, the incident took place at around noon. Now, before that event do you remember how many routes you'd already done along that line?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, I'd just taken over my shift, and I'd just started off from the depot towards Bascarsija. So it was the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous shift was on duty, and there were no remarks or comments made by them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we zoom in, please? Can we zoom in a bit more? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you can see here Marin Dvor and Skenderija. Does that help you find your bearings? Could you draw in the direction you were taking from the Zmaja od Bosne line.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do we need to move the map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: May I just take a moment to find my bearings on this map. I'm not very used to looking at maps. Zmaja od Bosne, here we are. Over here. I can see the railway line. It's difficult for me. I can't find my way around the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the incident after Marin Dvor or before Marin Dvor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: The incident took place before Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we're going to ask the technicians to move --

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: I can't see the S curve, the S bend where the incident took place, but Marin Dvor is very close by here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the incident took place on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: It was quite a bit before Marin Dvor, actually, and opposite the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it be moved more to the right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, I know from proofing this morning that the witness has a great deal of difficulty unless the font of something she sees is very large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. We'll zoom in, but I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think you need these markings. The witness was trying to find her way. So we can move the map and delete that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can now see Cengic Vila.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the beginning of Zmaja od Bosne. Now, a little to the left, and we get to the S curve or S bend. On the opposite side, right. Left. Bear left. Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you like us to zoom in a bit more to enlarge this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, can I see the letters a bit better? If we could have the letters enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I know that the S curve isn't yet -- that she's talking about isn't yet displayed on the map. You need to move a little bit further to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To the left or to the right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. I've always had an issue that way, Your Honour. That way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Move that way, please. No, no, no. The opposite way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Note -- Your Honour, if I may, that's -- now the S curve should be on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? I'm not quite clear with this map because the Miljacka River can't be seen at all in that area. That's what I don't understand. The railway line is over here, but I can't really see the part where the shots came from because this is the part of town on the right-hand side and on the right-hand -- when you're on the right-hand side, you can't see the river at all. You can see the Miljacka River from Skenderija. That's when tram runs along the Miljacka River, from Skenderija onwards. So up until Skenderija, the tram doesn't run along the river. You can't see the Miljacka River. Kuljina Ban, that embankment, there are tracks there, and the river's there. Well, I can see the S bend if this is the tram-railway line from Marin Dvor, but I think that it runs towards Cengic Vila.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: It's the left side. It's the side which runs from Carsija to the depot and not the side from the depot towards Carsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me: The Zmaja od Bosne Street, the tram runs in both directions there, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as you've described the event, the event took place right near the Holiday Inn hotel, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Along the route from Zmaja od Bosne and Franjo Ratko from the direction of the Miljacka River, and then it runs towards Zmaja od Bosne Street. So it's between the national museum, Zemaljski Museum, and then there's the Executive Council building and the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The "M" underneath where it says "Marin Dvor," is that the national Zemaljski Museum?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: The national museum, Zemaljski Museum is not by Marin Dvor at all, but maybe it is. You might be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Never mind. On this map where it says Zmaja od Bosne Street, just draw in the direction your tram was moving in. I assume you can do that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: I can't because this is in the opposite direction. It's leading from the Carsija, the centre of town, towards the depot. I can't see the tracks leading from the depot towards Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see the Zmaja od Bosne Street, and if so, could you mark in that street?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, draw an arrow in the direction your tram was moving.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: If this are -- if these are the tram tracks, then this would be it, like this, and that's the bend. But that -- well, that's not the bend, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Now, just an arrow to show the direction you were moving in. At the top of that line, just put in an arrow showing the direction.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it's clear from this map and that we can tender it into evidence and leave the witness alone. I think she's done the best she can, and I'm sure that on the basis of her testimony and statement we'll be able to determine all the different factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The map 65 ter 4448 as marked is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll now move on to the incident itself. In the first statement you gave immediately after the event, you gave it in the Sarajevo police station, and you said today that you had certain corrections to make with respect to the casualties. Now, you said at the time that you heard a blunt blow hitting the back part of the tram. Do you remember having said that? So -- but tell us, how did you know that the tram had been hit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, I heard the blow. I heard the hit. And it wasn't at the back of the tram, right at the back. It's by the third door because there's a space between the third door, and then there's the fourth door, the fourth doors, and then the back of the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll look at the crime report with the photographs, so the location is something we'll be able to see from that there, but I'm just interested in the sound you heard. You heard this sound, blunt blow in the back of the tram, the back part.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: I just heard the sound of the shot, and then the passengers said that the tram was hit, had been hit, was being shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear. You heard this blunt sound of a blunt blow.

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: But the tram that was moving in front of me, this blunt sound hit the cable above that tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see what direction it came from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Well, I can't say, but we know where it came from. It came from the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of the traces you saw in the tram, you made the conclusion that the bullet had come from that direction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, do you know that the BH army had the same sniper rifles or similar sniper rifles as the army of Republika Srpska did?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, how come you knew that it was Seselj's Chetniks, as you said, that were shooting from those positions? You said that you knew that was the case between you heard that Seselj had come visiting, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, you said that not all Serbs were the same as far as you were concerned, that there were differences between the Serbs, people who did things like that and others who didn't; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVICA LIVNJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour, for this witness. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, ma'am. That brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify at the Tribunal. We hope you travel well back home. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes -- that's my business before Your Honours today, and with your leave I'll take my leave, and I'll turn over the floor to my colleague Mr. Cannata for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're granted leave to take your leave, ma'am. You're excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Turn over to -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. If I might have your indulgence, I will just switch the work station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Cannata. Then we will see you better.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. Just a quick point of clarification prior to the next witness being called, if I might. I understand that the Prosecution intends to introduce a series of statements that this witness has made on a previous occasion with regard to their - as we're calling it for the moment - a 92 ter package. It is my understanding - which is why I'm asking for the point of clarification - it is my understanding that this witness is being called to testify about a particular scheduled incident, and if my understanding is correct, nothing more and nothing less. If that is the case, then I may have some comments with regard to some information that is contained in one of the statements because it does not pertain to the particular scheduled incident upon which this witness has been called. So that is just a brief point of clarification so that I'm able to deal with the evidence as it comes in. The second thing is it -- and I don't know how the Chamber views this. When Ms. Edgerton was giving us the summaries, she said that it was a summary of the evidence, and I had a little bit of a knot in my stomach, just a slight one, because as I understand the summaries, they're not evidence at all; but rather, they are a publication for the public's purpose so they have an understanding of, in fact, what the witness is generally testifying about, but they're not to be deemed to be evidence, and any summary that comes in is not deemed as evidence. I just wanted to make sure I was correct about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are absolutely correct, and that's how the Trial Chamber will regard those summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If she did say summary of the evidence, then she misspoke. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you sit down, speaking for myself, I do not understand the clarification you are seeking on the first point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if Mr. Cannata understood you, then I'll ask him to respond. Maybe I'll follow the clarification you seek if he does respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm quite sure I do understand the clarification as sought by my learned friend, but I would like him to clarify also. So I will wait for him to clarify what's the point of -- at issue here, and then I give you my response, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I understand you, then you are just in the dark like I am. What is your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact, he's not in the dark. He knows exactly what I'm talking about, but as -- as an advocate he wishes -- he wishes for me to commit, which I don't mind doing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I understand the testimony of this particular witness, it deals with a Scheduled Incident A, and I believe that it's number 6. To the extent that the witness's first statement resolves around that information, I, of course, have no concerns. To the extent that the Prosecution is relying on any other information concerning what could be deemed potentially an unscheduled incident, and by that I'm referring specifically to information as contained in paragraph 3 of the first witness statement, my question is: Is the Prosecution relying on that particular information, which is an unscheduled incident, as I understand it, for this particular trial? I think I've committed about as much as I can, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: The Prosecution acknowledges that there is a Rule 72 bis decision outstanding, so the Prosecution decides not to lead any evidence on the '93 incident that the Defence counsel has just referred to, which is the one referred to at paragraph 3 of the first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I'm clear about what they're doing, and I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. May you call your witness, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution calls Witness Enes Jasarevic. With your leave, Your Honour, while the witness is brought here, I give you a very short -- a brief summary of what I intend to do with this witness. Now, the witness is a 92 witness as anticipated by the Defence, and he gave two statements to the OTP in March 1997 and May 2006 and also testified before this Tribunal in the Dragomir Milosevic case. With your leave, we will go through the 92 ter procedure and we will seek the admission of these two statements and the transcripts. Now, to complete the procedure, we will then -- actually, after the procedure is completed, we will then read for the public and the record a very short summary, a real short one this time. And finally, with your leave, we will seek to ask some additional questions, very limited, and I hope to contain my examination within the 30 minutes as scheduled before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jasarevic. Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name, place, and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Enes Jasarevic. I was born in 1958 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, did you give two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, the first on 10 March 1997 and the second on 19 May 2006?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review these two statements in your own language before appearing today in court?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have had an opportunity to review them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the corrections, amendments, and clarifications that you made to your first statement on your second statement given to the OTP on 19 May 2006 in a language that you understand before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, with the corrections to the first statement made on the second statement given on 19 May in 2006, do you confirm that these statements are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. With those corrections, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I would move these two statements which are 65 ter 9270 and 9271 into evidence with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9270, 9271 are admitted into evidence. May they be please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 09270 will become Exhibit P37, Your Honours; and 65 ter 09271 will become Exhibit P38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, did you testify in case Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic on 1st of March, 2007? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review copy of your testimony in chief before this Tribunal in that case in a language you do understand? Did you?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to review the documents, namely maps and photographs, which were associated to the testimony in chief that you gave to this Tribunal in the Dragomir Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Witness, do you confirm, then, that the evidence that you gave in your testimony in chief and its associated exhibits are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do such evidence -- excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do such evidence - that is, the transcript and its associated exhibits - reflect your answers if you were to answer to the same questions again today?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I would move the transcripts and associated exhibits discussed into evidence, and for that purpose with your leave I can provide you with a list of 65 ter numbers. I will move into evidence 65 ter number 9277, which is the transcript of Witness Jasarevic's testimony in Dragomir Milosevic case, the highlighted parts which the Prosecution intends to rely upon. Then 65 ter 9272 would be the street map Sarajevo as marked by the witness; 65 ter 9273, again, an annotated map; 65 ter 3024.01, photograph; 3024.11, another photograph; 3024.2, another photograph; 3024.3, 3024.4, 3024. -- actually, 05. I have to make a correction. I'm sorry. After -- so the 65 ter 3024.2 should be recorded as 3024.02. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm getting confused with all this numbering. And then 3024.3 should be recorded as 3024.03; 3024.4 should be transcribed as 3024.04; 3024.05, another photograph; 3024.06 - I'm coming to an end now with your indulgence - 3024.08; and 3024.09; and the last one would be 9275, which is a street map again. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cannata. All those 65 ter documents are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number starting with 65 ter 9277.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 09277 will be Exhibit P39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 09272 will become Exhibit P40. 65 ter 09273 will become Exhibit P41. 65 ter 03024.01 will become Exhibit P42. 65 ter 03024.11 will become P43. 65 ter 03024.02 will become Exhibit P44. 65 ter 03024.03 will become Exhibit P45. 65 ter 03024.04 will become Exhibit P46. 65 ter 03024.05 will become Exhibit P47. 65 ter 03024.06 will become Exhibit P48. 65 ter 03024.08 will become Exhibit P49. 65 ter 03024.09 will become Exhibit P50. And finally, 65 ter 09275 will become Exhibit P51, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave at this point I would read out the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Witness Enes Jasarevic has given evidence in respect of Scheduled Incident A6 of the indictment, that is the incident occurred on 24 May 1995 in Majdanska Street in Sarajevo when two civilians were killed and at least six, including the witness himself, were wounded by the explosion of a modified air bomb. During the period 1994 to 1995, the witness worked as an electrician for high-voltage power lines at the transformer station located in Majdanska Street in the Novi Grad municipality of Sarajevo. He testified that on 24 May 1995 at around 2.00 p.m., he and two of his colleagues, Salko Slato and Prasko Sulejman, were hit by the explosion of a bomb which impacted a pylon inside the compound of the transformer station. As a result of such explosion, Witness Jasarevic was wounded in his arm and legs. Salko Slato was slightly injured, and Prasko Sulejman was killed. The witness testified there were no military position anywhere near the transformer station. He also gave evidence that on 24 May 1995, he did not notice any fighting or military activity or military personnel in the vicinity of the transformer station. That is the summary of evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And I'm getting really close to the end of my examination, and with your leave if I can ask a few -- really, a few questions to clarify some matters in the previous statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Registrar, can we please have 65 ter 9245 on the screen, please. And while this is being uploaded, it's one of our Sarajevo maps contained in the court binder. Now, as Your Honour and the parties are aware, such an exhibit -- such a 65 ter number is part of our sixth supplemental exhibit list, and a decision for that application is still pending. So as I understand, this exhibit will be -- the Prosecution will ask to mark for identification this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which map in the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: It's the -- the one -- give me one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Map 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct. That's page 13, although I would ask Madam Registrar to zoom in -- actually, to zoom in a little bit right towards the centre of the map. Yes. I think that would be -- that should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see the map? Do you have a map on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you see the transformer station you were working at on the 24 May 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are asked to repeat your answer, sir. The witness -- the interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you please mark the transformer station with the marker that Madam Usher will provide you with and sign it with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] Is this all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness. How long have you worked at the transformer station in Majdanska Street, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: A year and a half, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: So are you familiar with the surroundings of the transformer station?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see -- do you recognise the big building behind the transformer station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking about the building immediately behind or where there are so many buildings behind the transformer station, Mr. Cannata?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you see the TV building here in this map?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with the letter "B." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Do you also see the municipality building in this map? Do you?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with the letter "C."

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see what seems to me a sort of light yellow building immediately in front of the transformer station? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with the letter "D."

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know, what is that building?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a school, a primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, do you also see next to the school building a group of high-rise buildings? Do you see them?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you please mark them with the letter "E."

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. What buildings are there? What kind of buildings are there?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Residential buildings. It's the Opacno [phoen] residential estate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, on the 24th May, 1995, was any of these building in the vicinity of the transformer station at Majdanska Street which you marked as letter "A"? Was any of them a military facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I object on the grounds of leading. I'm going to object on the grounds of leading. He can describe what the buildings were. It may well be outside of his knowledge, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sorry. I might re-ask the same question for each of the buildings I asked the witness to mark, and I think that would be a legitimate question to ask the witness whether, for instance, the municipality building was a military target or a -- sorry, I'll rephrase. A military facility. That's, I think, within the allowed lines of questioning. Now, for the sake of time, I have, let's say, consolidated a set of questions in just one question. But if Your Honour prefers, I can definitely go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, 1995, Mr. Jasarevic, have you noticed any military personnel or military activity in the vicinity of the transformer station at Majdanska Street?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not notice any military units or any -- anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cannata. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to first of all ask you some -- can you not hear?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I can hear now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to first of all ask you some questions concerning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, your opposite number is on his feet. Yes, Mr. Cannata. You want to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I really apologise for -- with all these markings and questions, I forgot the most important thing. The Prosecution would like to then tender the marked map into evidence, and I'm really sorry to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The map as marked is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Again, it would be a marked -- a marked-for-identification document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's marked for identification, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map marked by the witness, Your Honours, will become Exhibit P52 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry about that, Mr. Guy-Smith. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about your statement, and by that I'm referring to the first statement that you made, the statement that you ultimately corrected, and that would be -- and we don't need to bring it up yet. That would be Exhibit P37. What I'd like to know is this: Could you explain to the Chamber how you went about making that statement? And by that, I mean were you involved in an interview with some folks, and as they were talking to you they were writing down what you said and you confirmed it; or did you talk to them for a period of time and come back at a later point in time and they handed you a statement? Could you tell us how the statement was created?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I was invited to make a statement. I said what had happened on that day. There were two people present, a man and a woman who was interpreting. I didn't write the statement then. I was invited again, but I really can't recall when that was. And when I saw the statement, some things were not the way I had told them, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say when you saw the statement, I want to go back now, and if we could -- if we could pull up Exhibit P37 because you said you weren't sure when you -- you saw the statement or when you made the statement. I want to see whether this is of any help to you. And if we could just look at the -- I think it would be -- it would be the third page of the statement. Could we have the third page, please. Thank you. Do you recognise that signature as being your signature?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the date that you made the statement, and by that I mean the date you signed the statement was on the 10th of March, 1997, correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. It was a long time ago. And at that point in time, before you -- before you signed the statement, you had an opportunity to take a look at it and go through it. You were satisfied with it, I guess, because you signed it, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really remember this statement that well. That's why I corrected it later on because it wasn't the way I -- well, it was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when -- sorry, sir. You were about to say something. I didn't mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it that after you signed the statement in March of 1997, you didn't have any further contact with an investigator or member of the Prosecution until 2006, some nine years later, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in 2006, at that point in time when you met with them, and I think you met with them in May of 2006, at that point in time did they give you your old statement, you looked at it and you went, "Wow, that thing I signed nine years ago, there's some mistakes in it"? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I said there were some things there that I hadn't said in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That you -- that you hadn't said in that way. And when you -- back in 1997 when you -- when you made your statement and before you signed it, did you get a chance to read your statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I read it or not. I really don't. But there were certainly some things in it that weren't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how they got there? Since -- if you didn't say them, do you know how they got there?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably the young lady who was interpreting, she was the one writing it down. Whether she was doing it properly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just want to stay for a moment with this statement in 1997, which we know you've corrected. At that point in time, which you've just told us is perhaps she was writing things down, but before you signed the statement, did somebody go through the statement with you, maybe not word by word but certainly line by line or paragraph by paragraph to ensure that the information contained in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I think the same question has been asked, maybe on the -- in different words, but the concept is clear. It has been asked to the witness. Page 37, line 10: "When you made your statement, and before you signed it" - and I'm quoting - "did you get a chance to read your statement in your own language?" And the witness said, "I don't remember." I wonder whether there's any point in going through this same question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might respond, Your Honour. It's a slightly different question by virtue of the witness's answer because from what I understood his answer to be - and I had one question in this regard and then I'm finished with this area - was that the statement was created, I guess by the person who was writing stuff down, and so I'm wondering whether or not he had a chance to just have somebody go through it line by line, and then I'm done in this area. But if the Chamber's satisfied where we are, I'm satisfied. Otherwise, it's just dealing with a different way. As opposed to the internal reflection of looking at the statement, it would be the -- it would be the verbal contact between two people as they're reviewing the statement itself. It's to make sure that the information contained therein would be accurate. It would be one of the ways that people go through an interview process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only question is that the witness says he doesn't remember, but ask the question. Let's find out whether that jogs his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not as you were going through the first statement, did you have an opportunity to have somebody go through it with you line by line or paragraph by paragraph so you could confirm, deny, or modify the information that is contained within each of the paragraphs before you signed it? If you remember, great. If you don't remember, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember that somebody did that with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Between the time that you signed your first statement and the time that you had second contact with the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006, did you have occasion to spend any time watching any of the proceedings that occurred here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean on television?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes. Occasionally by chance, but not regularly. Just the sort of bulletins.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before you testified in the previous case, did you have occasion to talk to anybody about bombs in general and your experience with them in specific apart from the statement that you made in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I've had no experience with any bombs. Who could I talk to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My internal clock is getting somewhat better, and I believe based on the Chamber's estimation now would be an appropriate time for a break. I think it's been an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very right, Mr. Guy-Smith. We'll take a break and come back at half past 5.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Chamber about what the function is of a transformer like the one that you were at on May 24th, 1995? What does a transformer do?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, a transformer station uses power lines, long distance power lines, and it's a 110-kilowatt energy voltage, high voltage, and then a transformer reduces the level and provides the electricity for the population. So that would be its basic function.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo, was there more than one transformer that was being used for the purpose that you've just said, which is to provide electricity during the time that you were working?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were several. This particular one couldn't cover all the needs. It was just for a part of town. So, yes, there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you -- could you tell us how many transformers there were in the city of Sarajevo, if you know, during 1995?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean the ones that were operational? There weren't any long distance power lines for some areas, so they had to use cables and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do mean it as you've suggested, the ones that were operational. How many operational transformers were there?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly it was just one or two that were operational, and we received high voltage electricity from them, and then this would be relayed to the others through cables and so on, but it wasn't sufficient to supply the entire city.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were working on the power lines in 1995, many times that you were working it was as a result of the power lines being damaged or destroyed because of fighting between the various armies, correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, because there was an interruption in the system due to the war going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And on occasions, one of the targets that you had to repair in your capacity as the repairman on the power lines was a targeted power line or a pylon that one or the other of the warring factions had targeted for an attack, correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. Mostly one side because the other side, it wasn't in their interest to cut off the power supply because we'd have to repair it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And the side who it wasn't in their interest to cut off the power supply, that would have been the Bosnian army, right? They needed that power supply in order to -- in order to function, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way. It was the citizens that needed the power supply. I don't know about the BH army, but the city needed electricity and a power supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. To your knowledge, was the BH army in the city itself in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Whether the army was in the city, is that what you're asking, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the army used the electricity that came from the transformers that were in the city, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know what electricity it used and where the electricity went. I'm just telling you how it was distributed, with the cables. Now, what it was used for, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were involved in repairing power lines and I assume working on the transformer, also, did you ever have occasion to go to an area where the Bosnian army was billeted and do any electric repair in such an area?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't repair things where the soldiers were, just where the break had occurred. And there were pylons, power lines that were cut off, and you went there. There were no soldiers there. Well, I don't know. Perhaps we were at some separation line at times, but not -- but not where UNPROFOR was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not where UNPROFOR was. Now, UNPROFOR on occasion, if I understood your previous testimony, would on occasion escort you to areas where there were broken lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, that's right, because otherwise we couldn't go there. We couldn't go there without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Could it be made clear, Mr. Guy-Smith, what broken lines -- what we mean by "broken lines"? There's been a separation -- a question of lines, separation --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and power lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When we're talking about broken lines, I'm not referring to the breaking of a front line in the military sense but, rather, a broken line in terms of an electrical line, a power line, correct? So when I use the word "broken lines" - point well taken - we're discussing the -- a line that moves energy from one part -- from one point to another point through -- after having been modified through the transformer, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when there was -- when there was fighting going on, UNPROFOR would not escort you to an area where there may be the necessity of some repair, correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies. It was badly phrased. Let me try again. When you were going to go repair an electric line, you were escorted by UNPROFOR, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When there was fighting going on, then you did not go repair the lines, the electric lines, because among other things, UNPROFOR did not escort you to the area where you may do such repair, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That was mostly it. They would inform us when they were ready and when they could go or could not go. We didn't know the reasons, but they said we can't go and then we didn't go and do our repair work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, on May 24th, that was the day that you were going to do some repair work, but you received information from UNPROFOR that they would not be escorting you on that day, right?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They would just say no mission, cancel it, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in 1999, when NATO bombed Belgrade, that one of its targets, one of its main targets were the transformers in the city of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, that that was the main target, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, not the main target, one of the main targets was the transformers in the city, the same kinds of transformers that we've been talking about here today.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of transformers being their target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that when NATO bombed Belgrade in 1999, transformers in the city of Belgrade were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either. No, it's not something that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you for your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before I turn it over to Mr. Cannata, can I ask you: Did you observe on any one occasion fighting going on in the city of Sarajevo during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in a position to notice whether there was fighting going on or not. Even when I went to the area where there was some combat, when I got there, there was a truce, so there wasn't any. No, not in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's understand the question. I'm not asking you whether you were in a position to notice. I'm asking you, did you -- did you observe any fighting at all in the city of Sarajevo during this period that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't notice anything like that. I wasn't in that kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With your leave, one question. Let's say a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, you've been asked about how many transformer stations were operational in Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: You said one or two. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Out of how many transformer stations are we talking about? How many transformer stations were in Sarajevo? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember -- let me just take a moment to count them if I may. About 16 or 17 were operational before the war, specifically in Sarajevo, because each part of town, each larger district had to have 110 feeds to cover the area because one or two couldn't cover the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. So only one or two out of the 16 or 17 transformer stations in Sarajevo were operational at the time which we are concerned with, which is mainly 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the others were not operational. We received electricity from just one direction. So the others couldn't have been functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And why is that, sir? Why only one or two transformer stations were operational?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, because Sarajevo doesn't have any energy source. So it has to receive the energy source from hydroelectric power plants or thermoelectric power plants, and they need long distance power lines, and all that was covered by the other side, so all you could get was what they let you have, and that long-distance transmission line was the only one that was functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: What do you mean by the other side? Can you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, let me explain it. From the Kakanj thermoelectric power plant, there's no pylon or long distance transmission line leading to Sarajevo. There's one in Vogosca and there's one in Blazuj and Raljevo, and the same transformer stations are then used to transmit electricity to us in town so that you could only receive as much as they let through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: So your evidence is that the electricity in Sarajevo was mainly based on what the city could receive from the surrounding hills, from the outside of the city lying in the valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct because we didn't have a power line that would reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Would the operations of just one or two transformer stations in Sarajevo be sufficient to provide the whole city of Sarajevo with enough electricity for daily survival?

utterances.speaker: ENES JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not even close. Let me tell you this way: If I said there were 16 or 17 of them that were usually needed for providing consumers with electricity, then it's as if you had just one glass of water to quench the thirst of ten people. They could just have a little, but you couldn't quench their thirst with just one glass of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cannata. Mr. Jasarevic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to testify. You are now excused. You may stand down, and may you travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: May I be excused for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused for one moment only.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be short. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're rising, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, that is the last witness whom the Prosecution was able to arrange to bring here this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you don't have one tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you will have one on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Monday the 27th, Your Honour, of October, because we understand that the next two weeks we have no -- no trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: However, Your Honours, I have one administrative matter that I would like to raise with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May we move into private session for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other issues by way of housekeeping from any party? None. That being the case, then the case stands adjourned to Monday, the 27th of October at 9.00 in the morning in courtroom 2. Court adjourned.
